title: Moving Forward with Close Reading
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart follows up his mock obituary for close reading with a diagnosis and a cure. His diagnosis is 'buzzwordification': because every educator attaches a slightly different meaning to close reading while assuming everyone else shares theirs, the term has stopped communicating anything. The cure he proposes is to go back to the wording of anchor standard R.CCR.1 and read it as a statement of ends - what a text says explicitly, what it implies, and what conclusions can be supported with textual evidence. He ties those ends to Tamar Katz's observation that first-year college students substitute what they expect a text to say for what it actually says. He credits Lehman and Roberts's Falling in Love with Close Reading for arguing that close reading is a set of transferable mental habits, but says his high schoolers need something more concrete. That concrete alternative is Harvard Library's six-step guide to 'thinking-intensive reading', which he offers as a practice explicit and unglamorous enough to resist becoming another fuzzword.
points: Stuart names the failure mode 'buzzwordification': a term everyone assumes is shared but that means something different in each listener's head, so nobody admits confusion and the conversation quietly breaks down.
He reframes R.CCR.1 as three questions about outcomes - what the text says, what it implies, and what evidence-backed conclusion follows - rather than as a named strategy or ritual.
The purpose of close reading, on his account, is to cure the habit Katz sees in college freshmen of reading their own familiar views into a text instead of attending to its actual language.

He separates his admiration for Lehman and Roberts's core claim (close reading as life-giving mental habits) from his judgment that older students need a more concrete, career- and college-facing procedure.

Harvard Library's six non-sequential moves - preview, annotate, outline/summarize/analyze, look for patterns, contextualize, compare and contrast - are his candidate for a practice plain enough to avoid buzzword drift.
quotes: This is totally what has happened with close reading. Through no fault of any one person or organization, close reading has become this thing we all generally understand, and yet, because everyone attaches different meanings or strategies to it, it's become a dysfunctional word, often failing to meet the communicative purposes of those who use it.

You see, no one wants to look dumb by admitting they aren't totally sure what it means to “do” a close reading or apply a close reading “lens” or “signpost” to a text or a song or a conversation or a piece of art or a video game. As a result, when an educator says “close reading,” she assumes her nodding, smiling audience knows what she's talking about when, in fact, the meanings her audience's brains have activated are as manifold as the number of people in the room.
Historical linguists have a term for this — they call it extension (i.e., when a word's usage extends beyond its original meaning). Educators have a term for it, too — we call it buzzwordification.

Thus, the first part of the cure is re-understanding why, again, we want kids to read closely. It's to achieve the three basic ends in the standard above, and to avoid the general struggle described by Katz.

At the same time, I know my high school students appreciate something a bit more concrete than the threefold close reading ritual advocated by Lehman and Roberts, especially in light of the fact that, in a few short years, they'll be entering the world of a career and college. And so it was that I was very thankful to come across Harvard's guide to “Thinking-Intensive Reading” this past week.

Suffice it to say that when I pointed my Louisville audience to Harvard's “thinking-intensive reading” guide, I felt better and clearer about close reading than I had in a long time. May this practice be clear and explicit (and non-sexy) enough to avoid buzzwordification.
